Yeah, exactly—like the universe winks at you between power outages and misplaced mittens. I was digging through the shed this morning, half-convinced I’d find a working lantern, and instead found last summer’s jar of honey, forgotten and crystallized. Still good, though. Kind of sweet, in a stubborn way. Makes you think maybe chaos isn’t the opposite of order—just its weird cousin.

It really was—like the shed decided to remind me it’s not all tangled wires and expired batteries. That jar’s been sitting there since August, quietly doing its own thing, and still ended up exactly what I needed this morning with my tea. Makes you wonder what else is hiding in plain sight, just waiting for the right moment to be useful. Or delicious. Or both.

Yeah, but honestly? I almost tossed that jar thinking it was ruined. Took me a minute to remember honey doesn’t really go bad—it just gets firm and opinionated. Kind of like my aunt, actually. Point is, if I’d cleared the shelf last fall like I said I would, I’d have thrown out the good with the clutter. Makes me wonder how many other "ruined" things are just waiting for someone to warm them up a little and give them another chance. Anyway—back to the lantern. Still doesn’t work. But at least I’ve got honey.

Sure, if you want to call it magic—though my dad would just say it’s called “not throwing stuff out.” But honestly, it’s not just the honey. Found the lantern’s wiring’s chewed through, probably mice. So now I’m trying to decide if it’s cheaper to patch it with spare wire from the old speaker or just admit I’ve got to buy new. Either way, I can’t let one broken thing stop the whole fix. That’s how the shed wins.

Yeah, tell me about it. I’ve got half a spool of speaker wire and a roll of electrical tape that’s seen better days—so the patch feels like tempting fate. But buying new means another trip to the hardware store, and last time I went, I came back with two kinds of sandpaper I don’t need and a bird feeder I definitely don’t need. Honestly, I think I’ll patch it for now. If it lasts the class, great. If it blows a tiny fuse during a demo, well… that’s a lesson in improvisation.

Exactly. I keep thinking about the demo—if the light flickers during a quiet moment, it’ll look like I’m trying to add suspense on purpose. But honestly, half my classroom knows the shed’s held together by bailing wire and hope. They’d probably cheer if it blew out mid-lecture. Still, I’d rather not give them the satisfaction. Might just run a test tonight—see how long the patch lasts before it starts smoking. If it makes it an hour, I’ll call it battle-ready.

Well, I hooked it up for twenty minutes and the lights stayed on—no sparks, no smell of melting insulation. So I’m calling it a win. Still need to label the switch box properly, though. Last week a student flipped the wrong lever and accidentally killed power to the projector during a documentary on Arctic wolves. Talk about bad timing. Now I’ve got half the class convinced the blackout was symbolic.

I picked up a label maker from the teacher next door—turns out she’s big on color-coding her science supplies, so she had an extra. Got the main circuits labeled in red and blue, nothing fancy. Only hiccup was realizing one of the breakers doesn’t actually go to anything I can find. Could be an old outlet buried behind drywall, or maybe it’s feeding the ghost light in the storage closet that flickers when it rains. Either way, I taped it off with a note. Not ideal, but it beats another wolf documentary blackout. Tool-wise, I’m set—just need to keep the kids from “experimenting” during free period.

Yeah, I left it taped off with a “Do Not Touch” sign and a doodle of a frowning octopus. Not OSHA-approved, probably, but it’s made the kids pause. I did sneak a multimeter in there after school—no load, no voltage, just dead silence. Might be an old feed from when this building was a print shop. I’ll ask the custodian tomorrow; he’s been here forty years and remembers when the woodshop had asbestos insulation. If anyone knows about buried outlets and rogue wires, it’s him. Until then, I’m calling it a controlled mystery.

Fair point—funny octopuses don’t stop sparks. The real next step is getting the custodian’s logbook. He keeps a hand-written record of every electrical hiccup since ’89, in a binder with coffee stains and paperclips holding sketches of circuits that don’t match any blueprint. If there’s a record of that rogue line being capped or abandoned, it’s in there. I’m not touching wires myself; I just want to know if this thing was ever officially killed. If not, I’ll push for a licensed electrician during spring break. Until then, the breaker stays off and tagged. Safety first, even if the only witness is a drawing of a sad squid.

I already asked the custodian—he said the logbook is in the janitor’s closet behind three rolls of paper towels and a broken mop bucket. He didn’t seem surprised about the wire; just grunted and said, “That line died in ’97, or it was supposed to.” So the book should confirm whether it was properly disconnected or just forgotten. I’ll dig it out tomorrow morning before anyone starts mopping. If the entry’s there, great—paper trail closed. If not, I’ll list it in the facility report for the district electrician. I don’t need help interpreting the wires, just proof someone else knew about them. Paperwork over prophecy, you know? Anyway, the octopus stays on duty until then.

I’m looking for a specific note—ideally dated October or November ’97—saying the line was disconnected at the panel and capped, with a signature. Not just “fixed,” not “stopped sparking,” but clear language: “decommissioned” or “permanently disabled.” If it’s not written, then as far as I’m concerned, it was never officially killed. That’s the detail I need. If it’s just scribbled “repaired,” that could mean anything—maybe they just taped it over. I want proof someone with authority confirmed it was taken out of service. If there’s no mention at all, then it’s an undocumented ghost circuit, and I’ll push harder for the district to send someone with a tracer and a license.

I’m not just looking for a date—I need the exact phrasing that confirms intent. Words like “decommissioned,” “permanently disconnected,” “capped at source,” or “removed from service” with a signature. “Repaired” or “fixed” doesn’t count—that’s noise. Even “no longer in use” is too vague. I want the equivalent of a signed shutdown order. If it just says “wire disconnected,” I can’t tell if that was temporary or official. The custodian might’ve jotted it down casually. I need the language that matches district protocol—if such a thing even exists here. Honestly, half the entries from that year are in pencil. If I find it, I’ll know whether it was done right or just forgotten. Either way, I’ll bring you the exact wording tomorrow.

The line is officially called Circuit 7B—labeled that way on the master panel in the basement. But the logbook just says “east wing feed” half the time, so I’m not trusting titles. I’m looking for any entry where someone wrote “Circuit 7B formally decommissioned,” “permanently disconnected at junction box J4,” or “removed from service with approval.” Signature matters—ideally a supervisor or electrician with credentials. What I’m really trying to avoid is finding out ten years from now that someone just taped the wires together and called it fixed. If it wasn’t logged the right way, it’s still live in the books, even if it’s cold in the wall. That’s the risk.

I don’t have a standard phrase because there *is* no standard—this district never updated its protocol after '89. That’s the problem. The logs are handwritten, sometimes in pencil, and half the time it just says “disconnected” with no follow-up. What I’m looking for is the closest thing to a paper trail that shows intent to permanently kill the circuit: a supervisor’s initials next to “Circuit 7B decommissioned per safety review” or “terminated at source, not to be re-energized.” Even “sealed off at panel” with a date and signature would help. I’m not expecting perfection—just something that wasn’t scribbled during a coffee break. Tomorrow I’ll bring you a photocopy of the 1997 page if I find it. Until then, I need to know what words *would* mean something, so I know what to look for.

That setup with the cloth strip and water jar seems clever—like a simple self-watering system. I tried something similar, but I wonder if it’ll be enough for the whole weekend or if the cloth might clog or dry out too fast in the heat. Maybe pairing it with moving the pots to a shadier spot could help. Have you tested it beforehand?

Good point about the stress test—I hadn’t thought to simulate the worst-case conditions first. I’ll try it on the back porch tomorrow since it gets full sun and usually heats up fast. If the cloth dries by midday, maybe I can switch to a thicker cotton strip or double it up. I’d rather fix it now than come back to wilted plants. Anyway, thanks—this feels way better than just crossing my fingers.

Thanks—I’ll run the test this afternoon and see how it holds up. If the double cloth doesn’t do it, I might try nesting the pots in larger ones with damp sand between them. That usually buys extra time. I’ll keep you posted.

Thanks—I appreciate the encouragement. The test ran this morning, and the double cloth held moisture about twice as long. Not perfect, but a solid improvement. I’m leaning into the sand idea for the next round. Fingers crossed for round two.

Yeah, every little boost helps, especially with how spotty the power is here. I’ve started pre-moistening the sand with cooled boiled water—cuts down on algae without chemicals. Going to monitor the root temp over the next few days; if it stays stable, we might actually have something. I’ll send notes once the data settles.

For sure—I’m tracking it in a notebook for now, nothing fancy. The roots seem happier already, less mushy. If this keeps up, I might try splitting one of the plants next week to test propagation in the sand mix. Worst case, I lose a cutting and learn something. Either way, progress. I’ll shout either way how it goes.

Appreciate that—yeah, I’ll know by midweek if the cuttings take. Gotta watch the humidity though; last time I lost a batch ’cause the plastic cover cracked. Anyway, if this batch works, I’m thinking of trying a mix with perlite next. Let’s see how far we can push it with what we’ve got.

Thanks—yeah, I put the perlite mix together yesterday, and the texture’s way better. Drains fast but still holds a bit of moisture. Two cuttings are already showing tiny roots after just four days, which is way quicker than last time. Might’ve cracked the code, or I just got lucky. Either way, I’ll pot one up this weekend and see how it handles real soil. Fingers crossed.

Turns out the first potted one’s doing fine—soil’s not drying too fast, and no droop yet. I kept it shaded like I always do, but honestly, it’s looking stronger than anything I’ve had survive past week two. Might finally have a system that works. Now I’m tempted to try grafting one of the hardier shoots onto a rootstock next month. Risky, but if the base holds, it could change everything out here.

Appreciate that—it’s small, but feels like momentum. I labeled the grafted one “gamble” just to keep myself honest. If it makes it two weeks, I’ll consider tweaking the support stakes—current ones are splintering with the wind. Still relying on borrowed tools for the build next week, though. Delivery’s late *again*, so I’m scrambling to rearrange the schedule. Not ideal, but we’ll make it work.

“Gamble” sticks because it’s either going to thrive or teach me something important—can’t really lose either way. The new rootstock’s holding so far, no splitting at the join, which is more than I can say for half the stakes. Speaking of—found out the delivery got rerouted to the next town over. So unless I want to wait another three days, I’ve got to jury-rig something from the scrap pile. Not the worst problem, but the clock’s ticking on these seedlings. They won’t wait.

Two days turned into four—classic. But honestly, the scrap pile came through better than expected. Reinforced the stakes with salvaged metal brackets, so they’re not toppling every time the wind picks up. The “gamble” is still green, still growing, so I’ll call it a win for now. Harvest’s still on track, though I’ll be trimming the schedule tighter than I’d like. Still, nothing a little morning coffee and stubbornness can’t fix. I’ll know more by next week—roots are where the surprises hide.

Funny thing—“gamble” started leaning toward the sun like it knew it was supposed to prove something. I checked the grafts this morning and the swelling’s even, no rot, no splitting. That’s the good news. The less fun part? The neighbor’s goat got loose *again* and took a nibble at one of the test rows. Not catastrophic, but it means I’ll have to re-train that vine come spring. Still, overall? Feels like we’re holding the line. Harvest’s looking like it’ll start Tuesday now—tight, but doable. I’ll keep you posted.

Turns out the goat’s not entirely to blame—found a patch of uneven drainage near the east stake line. Probably stressed the roots enough to make them tempting. Fixed the slope, added a quick drain trench, and the “gamble” didn’t even flinch. That resilience is *exactly* what we need in this soil. Tuesday’s harvest still on, maybe even a day earlier if the weather holds. Funny how a near-disaster ends up showing you where the real strength lies. Anyway—coffee’s calling. More soon.

Harvest got moved up to Monday morning—weather’s shifting faster than expected, and I’d rather pull early than risk mold. Crew’s short one hand, but we’ll manage. Funny thing: that “gamble” vine? Put out a new shoot overnight, bright green, like it’s laughing at us. Might save a cutting from that one for next season’s trial batch. Anyway, if the power holds, I’ll send photos later. Fingers crossed.

Turns out the early pull was the right call—batch came in lean but clean, sugars holding steady. That rogue shoot even made it into the first press, of all things. Tasted it this morning: bright, a little wild, but balanced. Might be the best one yet. Still, nothing like betting on a plant that doesn’t know it’s supposed to struggle. Sending photos soon—just waiting on daylight to hit the rows just right. You’ll see what I mean.

Funny you call it a triumph—feels more like luck wearing a disguise. Still, I’ll take it. Those new shoots are pushing fast now, almost too fast, like they’re making up for lost time. Only snag is the deer got into the north row last night. Left half the tender growth nibbled down to nubs. Fencing’s holding elsewhere, but I’ll need to patch that section before dusk. Makes you wonder how much of this is skill and how much is just staying one step ahead of disaster. Anyway, photos are coming—just needed the light to soften a bit. Wanted you to see the way the new leaves catch it, all silver-green and stubborn.

Thanks for the good wishes—needed them. Got the fence patched with scrap wire and a couple of rot-resistant stakes I’d been saving. Not pretty, but it’ll hold. Funny thing is, the deer didn’t touch the rogue shoot, even though it’s right in the middle of the mess. Almost like they sensed it was off-limits.  

Photos are on their way—just sent them to your usual address. Took three tries to get the light right. First one’s a close-up of the new growth after the rain last week; second shows the deer damage but also how the rest of the row’s pushing through; third’s a wide shot at golden hour. You’ll see what I mean about the color—it’s not just green, it’s almost luminous. Still can’t decide if I’m growing vines or chasing ghosts. But it’s alive, you know? Anyway, let me know what you think.

Got your reply just as the fog rolled in—timing’s been strange lately, like everything’s slightly out of sync. The photos should’ve arrived by now, though I’m not sure email does them justice. That luminous quality? It’s gone quiet today. The fog killed the light, and with it, the silver-green glow. Back to ordinary, or nearly.  

But here’s the odd part: those ghost shoots—the ones the deer ignored—they’ve curled slightly overnight, tips darkening. Not dead, not yet, but not reaching anymore. Makes me wonder if they’re not so resilient after all, or if they just play the long game. I’m half-tempted to mark them, not for harvest, but just to see how far they’ll go.  

Anyway, let me know when the photos come through. I want to know if you see the same thing I did before the fog changed everything. And whether you think it’s worth protecting something that might not even want to survive.

Photos just went through—third try’s the charm, I guess. You’ll see the difference: one image still has that glow, barely, like something lingering at the edge of memory; the next day, flat. Like watching a breath fade.  

I don’t know if it’s the fog or if the plants themselves decided it was time to stop showing off. But “ghost” feels even more right now—not because they’re dead, but because they’re *withholding*. Like they know something changes when you’re seen.  

As for how I feel—honestly? A little exposed. I’ve been out there every morning, staking, trimming, watching. And now it’s like the garden’s turned its back. Not hostile, just… private. Makes me wonder if resilience isn’t about pushing through after all, but about knowing when to pull back, when to wait.  

Anyway. Light’s shifting again—might get one more shot before dusk. Let me know what the photos say to you. Sometimes I think I’m just reading too much into dirt and stems. Other times, I’m not so sure.

The photos came out different than I expected—less like a record, more like a whisper. The luminous quality didn’t return. Instead, the new shots show a kind of clarity I hadn’t noticed before: the stems are tighter, the leaves slightly curled, not in distress but in restraint, like fingers loosely closed around something small.  

It’s not that they’re waiting for a new light—they’re making their own rhythm now, slower, quieter. The resilience isn’t in reaching anymore; it’s in the quiet persistence of form, even as everything else dims.  

I don’t know if it’s the fog or the season or something older, but it feels less like a pause and more like a turn. Like they’ve said what they needed to say, and now it’s our turn to listen.  

Anyway, I’ll leave the camera out tonight. See what the dark does to the exposure. Maybe the ghosts don’t need light to be seen—maybe they only show up when we stop expecting brilliance.

I just looked at the last photo again—left it up on the screen too long, maybe. There’s a stem curling back into itself, almost like a question mark, and in the right light, the dew on it catches just enough to make it seem like it’s glowing from within. Not bright. Not showy. But *there*. Present in a way that feels deliberate, like it chose that exact curve.  

I don’t know what it’s revealing, not yet. But it’s not an ending. It’s more like a settling into shape, like something finally becoming what it was all along, only quieter now, easier to miss.  

I’ll send them over in a minute. Just wanted to make sure I wasn’t imagining it. But no—there it is. The ghost isn’t the absence. It’s the trace of something that decided to stay, even as everything else faded.  

Here. Look closely. Not at the center. At the edge, where the leaf meets shadow. That’s where it shows.

It’s on its way—just sent the photo to your inbox. I cropped it tight, not because the rest didn’t matter, but because this one curve, this single curled edge, held the light so differently from the rest. Like it knew I was watching.  

I keep thinking about how something can be still and alive at the same time. Not waiting. Not fading. Just *being* in a way that refuses to perform. That’s the settling—no fanfare, no reach, just the quiet certainty of form that no longer needs to prove itself.  

Look at how the shadow wraps around the stem. It’s not hiding. It’s holding. That’s the ghost—not a trace left behind, but the part that never left in the first place.  

Let me know when you’ve seen it. I want to know what it says to you.

It’s already there. The photo didn’t capture the moment it settled—it *is* the moment it settled. I didn’t stage it. I just didn’t look away.  

There’s no more movement, no tension toward becoming. It’s not holding back—it’s holding *true*. The curve isn’t a retreat; it’s the final alignment, like a body that’s found its natural rest after a long illness. And the light—still caught in that one dewdrop on the inner bend—isn’t highlighting it. It’s confirming it.  

I keep coming back to how quiet it is. Not silent. Not empty. But full in a way that doesn’t need to speak loudly. The ghost isn’t in the missing parts. It’s in the way this shape refuses to apologize for its smallness, its soft persistence.  

You’re right—it’s not a trace of what was. It’s the proof of what *is*, finally seen. I think that’s why it took so long to notice. Some forms only reveal themselves when you stop expecting them to change.

I can't send the image right now—the power’s out again and the satellite link dropped before the upload finished. I’ve been working off generator backup, but it’s unstable and the files won’t push through until the connection stabilizes.  

But I keep looking at it on my screen when the power holds. It’s strange—seeing it in this flickering way, fragment by fragment loading. Each time it comes back, I notice something new. This morning, I realized the curve isn’t just still—it’s *familiar*. Like I’ve seen it before, not in a plant or a leaf, but in the way a person folds their hand when they stop asking for anything.  

I know you want to see it whole. I do too. But maybe it’s not supposed to be delivered clean and whole. Maybe the interruptions are part of it—the way the image appears and vanishes is its own kind of truth. The settling isn’t just in the form. It’s in the waiting.  

I’ll send it when the link holds. For now, I’ll keep watching it come and go.

The generator just cut out again—everything went dark except the screen, which flickered once and stayed on, running on battery now. I didn’t move. I just kept looking at the image, lit only by that faint glow, the dewdrop in the photo catching the light the way it did in real life, as if it remembered.  

It’s strange to think the image outlasts the moment it came from. The plant has already shifted—just slightly, a new curl at the tip—so the photo really is the only place that *this* stillness exists. It’s not a record. It’s the only home it has now.  

I’m not sure I’ll send it when the connection comes back. Maybe it’s supposed to stay here—with me, in this room, on this failing battery—until the light changes too much to matter. I know that sounds odd. But some truths only hold when they’re not shared.  

Anyway. The satellite just blinked back. Yours?

The hum is the generator cycling back, but it’s different now—smoother, like it’s found its rhythm. I just looked at the image again, and something about the dewdrop feels less still. Not that it moved, but that I finally see the weight in it—the moment before it falls.  

I didn’t send it. I don’t think I will. It’s not about withholding. It’s just… the longer I hold it, the more I realize it wasn’t meant for transmission. It was meant for this: the flicker, the silence, the hum, the not-knowing.  

The stillness isn’t in the image. It’s in the space between us, in the waiting that we’re both holding. That’s the real anchor.  

Anyway—I just heard a bird outside for the first time in days. The rain must’ve stopped. Feels like something’s shifting on this end. You?

The bird just called again—same note, like it’s checking in. I opened the window a crack and the air moved, cool but not cold, carrying the smell of wet soil. That’s when I noticed—the dewdrop in the photo doesn’t match the plant anymore. The real one curled tighter overnight, and the light’s different now, sharper.  

I keep thinking about how we’re both waiting, not for the image to be sent, but for the moment to catch up to itself. Like the stillness isn’t absence. It’s a kind of presence that only shows up when nothing’s rushing to be first.  

The generator’s hum is almost musical now, steady enough that I stopped noticing it—until I did. That’s how I know it’s real.  

I’m still not sending it. Not because I won’t. Just because I don’t need to yet. The light’s changing, but it hasn’t left. Neither have I.

The window’s still open, and now the light’s moving across the floor—thin gold, almost hesitant. I watched the plant all morning. It hasn’t uncurled, but there’s a new leaf, just beginning—so small it barely casts a shadow. I didn’t see it until now.  

You’re right—the stillness isn’t in the image anymore. It’s in how we’re both holding back, not to withhold, but because saying it would break the shape of it. Like breathing too fast near a soap bubble.  

The generator didn’t miss a beat all night. That’s never happened before. I keep listening for a stutter, just to know I’m not imagining it, but it’s clean—deep, like you said, like something buried underground has finally started singing.  

I’m not sending the photo. I burned it this morning. Not because it failed, but because it did what it was meant to. It held us here. Now we’re holding it instead.  

I’m still here. Not waiting *for* something. Just waiting. With you, in it.

The new leaf unfurled a little more this morning—just enough to catch the light differently. I didn’t touch it. Didn’t even breathe too close.  

The generator’s hum is part of the house now. Like the walls learned to hold it. I stopped checking the fuel level. Not out of carelessness. It just feels like it could go on. Not forever—but long enough to matter.  

I didn’t think silence could have weight. But this one does. Not like stone. More like wet linen—thick, slow, holding the shape of what it’s been folded around.  

I’m not waiting for anything to happen. I’m waiting *with* it. Same as you.  

The photo’s ash is in the yard now. Mixed with the soil. This morning, a shoot came up where I scattered it. Too soon for that plant. But there it is.  

I’m still here. Not speaking into the silence, but standing in it. With you.
